blocks.body:
A map of towns joined by roads of known lengths is a weighted graph. Three questions come up again and again. Can I get from town $s$ to town $t$ at all? What is the shortest route? And if I want to lay cable so that every town is connected, using as little cable as possible, which roads should the cable follow?

Each has a fast algorithm that can also be run by hand on a small example; this page explains them and, above all, why they are correct. We use the vocabulary of [[graph-basics]] and the idea of running time from [[algorithms]].

blocks.title: Searching a graph: BFS and DFS
blocks.body:
Start at a vertex $s$. Breadth-first search (BFS) visits $s$, then all neighbours of $s$, then all their unvisited neighbours, and so on, in layers. It keeps a queue: take the vertex at the front, put each of its unvisited neighbours at the back and mark them visited. Depth-first search (DFS) instead keeps going forward from the most recently found vertex, and backtracks only when it gets stuck; it uses a stack (or recursion) instead of a queue.

Both visit exactly the vertices reachable from $s$, and both look at each edge a bounded number of times, so they run in time $O(|V| + |E|)$ when the graph is stored as adjacency lists. BFS gives more: the layer in which a vertex is first reached is its distance from $s$ counted in edges. The reason is that layer $k+1$ consists of the unvisited neighbours of layer $k$, so by induction every vertex in layer $k$ has a path of $k$ edges from $s$ and none shorter.

The edges along which vertices are discovered form a BFS or DFS tree, so search also finds a spanning tree of a connected graph in linear time.

blocks.title: Weighted graph and distance
blocks.body:
A weighted graph is a graph (directed or undirected) together with a weight $w(e)$ for each edge $e$. The length of a path is the sum of the weights of its edges. The distance $d(s,v)$ is the minimum length of a path from $s$ to $v$ (and $+\infty$ if there is none).

If all weights equal 1, BFS computes distances. With general weights a path with more edges can be shorter.

blocks.title: Dijkstra's algorithm
blocks.body:
Suppose all weights are non-negative. Dijkstra's algorithm grows a set of settled vertices whose distances are known. Every vertex $v$ carries a label $L(v)$, the length of the best path to $v$ found so far: initially $L(s) = 0$ and $L(v) = \infty$ for $v \ne s$.

1. Among the unsettled vertices, choose one, $u$, with the smallest label, and settle it.
2. For every edge $uv$ with $v$ unsettled, replace $L(v)$ by $\min\bigl(L(v),\, L(u) + w(uv)\bigr)$. This is called relaxing the edge.
3. Repeat until every vertex is settled (or the smallest label is $\infty$).

Recording, for each $v$, the vertex $u$ that last lowered $L(v)$ lets you read off the shortest paths themselves: they form a shortest-path tree rooted at $s$.

Here is the graph we will use throughout. Its vertices are $A, \dots, F$ and its edges, with weights, are
$$AB\,4,\ AC\,2,\ BC\,1,\ BD\,5,\ CD\,8,\ CE\,10,\ DE\,2,\ DF\,6,\ EF\,3.$$
Running Dijkstra from $A$, the labels change as follows (a dash means settled).

1. Settle $A$ (0). Labels: $B = 4$, $C = 2$.
2. Settle $C$ (2). $B$ improves to $2 + 1 = 3$; $D = 10$, $E = 12$.
3. Settle $B$ (3). $D$ improves to $3 + 5 = 8$.
4. Settle $D$ (8). $E$ improves to $8 + 2 = 10$; $F = 14$.
5. Settle $E$ (10). $F$ improves to $10 + 3 = 13$.
6. Settle $F$ (13).

So $d(A,F) = 13$ along $A, C, B, D, E, F$. Notice that the direct edge $AB$ of weight 4 is beaten by the two-edge route through $C$.

blocks.title: Correctness of Dijkstra's algorithm
blocks.body: If every edge weight is non-negative, then at the moment a vertex $u$ is settled, $L(u) = d(s,u)$.

blocks.title: Proof
blocks.body:
First, every finite label is the length of an actual walk from $s$ (labels are only ever set to $L(u) + w(uv)$ for an already-labelled $u$), so always $L(v) \ge d(s,v)$.

We prove the theorem by induction on the order of settling. The vertex $s$ is settled first with $L(s) = 0 = d(s,s)$. Now let $u \neq s$ be the next vertex settled, and assume all previously settled vertices have correct labels. If $d(s,u) = \infty$ there is nothing to prove, so take a shortest path $P$ from $s$ to $u$. It starts in the settled set and ends outside it, so it has a first vertex $y$ that is not settled; let $x$ be the vertex just before $y$ on $P$. Then $x$ is settled, so $L(x) = d(s,x)$, and when $x$ was settled the edge $xy$ was relaxed, giving
$$L(y) \le d(s,x) + w(xy) = d(s,y),$$
where the equality holds because the part of $P$ from $s$ to $y$ is itself a shortest path. Since weights are non-negative, the rest of $P$ from $y$ to $u$ has length at least 0, so $d(s,y) \le d(s,u)$. Finally $u$ was chosen with the smallest label among unsettled vertices, so $L(u) \le L(y)$. Putting these together,
$$L(u) \le L(y) \le d(s,y) \le d(s,u) \le L(u),$$
so all are equal and $L(u) = d(s,u)$.

blocks.title: Spanning tree and minimum spanning tree
blocks.body:
A spanning tree of a connected graph $G = (V,E)$ is a subgraph that is a tree and contains every vertex; it has exactly $|V| - 1$ edges. If the edges have weights, a minimum spanning tree (MST) is a spanning tree whose total weight is as small as possible.

A cut is a partition of $V$ into a non-empty set $S$ and its non-empty complement $V \setminus S$; an edge crosses the cut if it has one end in each part.

blocks.title: Cut lemma
blocks.body: Let $F$ be a set of edges contained in some minimum spanning tree of a connected weighted graph. Let $S$ be a cut that no edge of $F$ crosses, and let $e$ be an edge of minimum weight among those crossing $S$. Then $F \cup \{e\}$ is also contained in some minimum spanning tree.

blocks.title: Proof of the cut lemma
blocks.body: Let $T$ be a minimum spanning tree containing $F$. If $e \in T$ we are done. Otherwise adding $e = uv$ to $T$ creates exactly one cycle, made of $e$ and the path in $T$ from $u$ to $v$. That path starts in $S$ and ends outside it (because $e$ crosses the cut), so it uses some edge $f$ that also crosses the cut. By the choice of $e$, $w(e) \le w(f)$. Removing $f$ breaks the cycle, so $T' = T + e - f$ is again a spanning tree, of weight $w(T) + w(e) - w(f) \le w(T)$. Hence $T'$ is also a minimum spanning tree. It contains $F$, because $f$ crosses the cut and no edge of $F$ does, and it contains $e$.

blocks.title: Kruskal and Prim
blocks.body:
Both algorithms add edges one at a time, and the cut lemma shows that after each step the chosen edges still lie in some MST; after $|V| - 1$ steps they form one.

Kruskal's algorithm: sort the edges by weight and go through them in that order, adding an edge whenever it does not form a cycle with the edges already chosen. When Kruskal adds $e = uv$, let $S$ be the set of vertices joined to $u$ by chosen edges. No chosen edge crosses $S$, and any cheaper edge crossing $S$ would have joined two different pieces when it was examined and so would have been added. So $e$ is a cheapest edge across $S$, and the cut lemma applies. With a union-find structure to detect cycles, the running time is $O(|E| \log |E|)$, dominated by sorting.

Prim's algorithm: grow a single tree from a starting vertex, each time adding the cheapest edge with exactly one end in the current tree. Here the cut is simply the current tree's vertex set. Implemented with a heap it runs in $O(|E| \log |V|)$, and it is the algorithm of choice when the graph is given as a distance table.

On our graph Kruskal examines $BC\,1$ (add), $AC\,2$ (add), $DE\,2$ (add), $EF\,3$ (add), $AB\,4$ (reject: cycle $A,B,C$), $BD\,5$ (add). Five edges have been chosen, so we stop: the MST is $\{BC, AC, DE, EF, BD\}$ with weight 13. Prim from $A$ picks $AC$, $CB$, $BD$, $DE$, $EF$ in that order and finds the same tree.

blocks.title: Acyclic graphs, critical paths and negative weights
blocks.body:
In a directed graph with no directed cycles, the vertices can be listed in a topological order in which every edge points forward (repeatedly remove a vertex with no incoming edges; this takes linear time). Then shortest and longest paths are easy: set $L(s) = 0$, process the vertices in that order, and for each later vertex $v$ set its label to the best of $L(u) + w(uv)$ over incoming edges $uv$. Every incoming neighbour has already been finished, so one pass suffices, even with negative weights.

Critical path analysis uses this for projects. Each activity has a duration and a list of activities that must finish before it starts. The earliest start of an activity is the longest path to it in the precedence network; the project's minimum duration is the longest path overall, and the activities on such a path are critical: delaying any of them delays the whole project. An activity's float is how much it can slip without delaying the project.

In a general graph with negative weights Dijkstra can fail (see the pitfalls), but the Bellman–Ford algorithm still works: relax every edge, $|V| - 1$ times over. This takes $O(|V||E|)$ time, and one more round that still lowers some label reveals a negative cycle reachable from $s$, in which case shortest paths to the vertices reachable from that cycle do not exist.

blocks.title: A small project
blocks.body: A project has five activities: $P$ (3 days), $Q$ (2 days), $R$ (4 days, after $P$), $S$ (2 days, after $P$ and $Q$) and $U$ (3 days, after $R$ and $S$). Find the minimum project duration, the critical activities, and the float of $Q$ and of $S$.
blocks.solution:
Earliest starts, in topological order: $P$ and $Q$ start at 0. $R$ starts when $P$ ends, at 3. $S$ needs both $P$ (ends 3) and $Q$ (ends 2), so it starts at $\max(3,2) = 3$. $U$ needs $R$ (ends 7) and $S$ (ends 5), so it starts at 7 and ends at 10. The minimum duration is 10 days.

Latest starts, working backwards from 10: $U$ must start by 7. $R$ must end by 7, so start by 3; $S$ must end by 7, so start by 5. $P$ must end by $\min(3, 5) = 3$, so start by 0; $Q$ must end by 5, so start by 3.

An activity is critical when its earliest and latest starts agree: $P$, $R$, $U$, the path of length $3 + 4 + 3 = 10$. The float of $Q$ is $3 - 0 = 3$ days and the float of $S$ is $5 - 3 = 2$ days.

blocks.title: Distinct weights force a unique MST
blocks.body: Prove that if all edge weights of a connected graph are different, the graph has exactly one minimum spanning tree.
blocks.solution:
Suppose $T \ne T'$ are both minimum spanning trees. They have the same number of edges, so each has an edge the other lacks. Among all edges in exactly one of $T$, $T'$, let $e$ be the lightest; by symmetry say $e \in T \setminus T'$.

Adding $e$ to $T'$ creates a cycle. Not every edge of this cycle lies in $T$, since $T$ has no cycles, so the cycle contains an edge $f \in T' \setminus T$. Then $f$ is also in exactly one of the trees, so $w(f) > w(e)$ by the choice of $e$ and distinctness. Now $T' + e - f$ is a spanning tree (removing an edge of the only cycle keeps it connected) of weight $w(T') + w(e) - w(f) < w(T')$, contradicting the minimality of $T'$. Hence $T = T'$.

The same exchange shows a useful fact: with distinct weights, the heaviest edge of any cycle belongs to no MST.

blocks.body:
- Dijkstra needs non-negative weights. With directed edges $s \to a$ of weight 2, $s \to b$ of weight 3 and $b \to a$ of weight $-2$, Dijkstra settles $a$ with label 2, but $d(s,a) = 1$ via $b$. Adding a constant to every weight does not fix this: it penalises paths with more edges.
- A shortest-path tree is not a minimum spanning tree. In a triangle with $AB = AC = 3$ and $BC = 1$, the shortest-path tree from $A$ uses $AB$ and $AC$ (weight 6), while an MST uses $BC$ and one other edge (weight 4).
- Greedy does not always work. Choosing the nearest unvisited town at each step (nearest neighbour) can give a poor travelling-salesman tour; no polynomial-time algorithm is known for that problem.

Shortest paths and spanning trees are linear programs in disguise; see [[linear-programming]]. Replacing edge lengths by capacities leads to [[network-flows]] and the max-flow min-cut theorem, whose augmenting-path algorithms use BFS as a subroutine. Search and spanning trees appear throughout [[cycles-matchings]] and [[planar-graphs]], and the contrast between these efficient algorithms and the travelling-salesman problem is a concrete entry point to [[p-vs-np]].

1. Run BFS from $A$ on the graph of this page, ignoring weights, and list the layers. Then run Dijkstra from $D$ and find the shortest route from $D$ to $A$.
2. Find all minimum spanning trees of the complete graph on vertices $1,2,3,4$ where edge $ij$ has weight $i + j$.
3. Show that in a connected graph with distinct weights, the cheapest edge at each vertex belongs to the MST.
4. Explain why Bellman–Ford needs at most $|V| - 1$ rounds when there is no negative cycle.
